title: Morning Edition
dek: Manila's alliance, Europe's power grids, island nations at climate talks, and what old books preserve.

lead_story.headline: US and Philippines announce expanded defence cooperation ahead of APEC
lead_story.summary: During a Manila meeting, President Trump said Washington was expanding military cooperation with the Philippines and discussed possible civilian nuclear-energy cooperation. Reuters reports that the administration cited more than $5 billion in approved arms sales; these are administration claims, not completed deliveries.
lead_story.why_it_matters: The alliance is central to security in the South China Sea, where Manila and Beijing have competing maritime claims.

items.headline: EU negotiators agree to faster renewable-energy and grid permits
items.summary: The Council and Parliament reached a provisional agreement to accelerate permits for renewable projects, electricity networks and storage. The rules still require formal adoption.
items.why_it_matters: Grid bottlenecks can leave wind and solar output unused even after generation capacity has been built.

items.headline: Small island states press COP31 for concrete climate finance
items.summary: At UN climate talks in Antalya, island representatives are asking wealthier emitters for stronger mitigation, adaptation funding and disaster-warning support. Negotiations remain open.
items.why_it_matters: Small island governments face high exposure to sea-level rise and extreme weather despite contributing little to cumulative emissions.

items.headline: Sudan's drone war brings attacks into markets and neighborhoods
items.summary: A Guardian investigation describes growing use of long-range drones by both sides in Sudan's war, with strikes killing civilians and disrupting essential services. Casualty totals and responsibility for individual attacks remain difficult to verify independently.
items.why_it_matters: Long-range systems expand the reach of the conflict and the risks faced by civilians far from conventional front lines.

items.headline: Corporate layoffs accumulate across Australia
items.summary: Reuters documents job cuts at multiple Australian companies in 2026, reflecting restructuring pressures across sectors. The pattern should not be mistaken for a single national employment statistic.
items.why_it_matters: Company-level decisions can signal shifting costs and investment priorities, but their national significance needs labor-market data.

items.headline: Older catch-up: medieval manuscripts preserve traces of a sheep virus
items.summary: Researchers recovered genetic traces of sheep pox from historic parchment and animal remains, showing that manuscripts can preserve evidence of livestock disease as well as human writing.
items.why_it_matters: Archives may hold biological records of the past that were never intentionally recorded.

items.headline: St. Catharines market prepares a neighborhood holiday fair
items.summary: The annual Light Up the Holidays vendor event is scheduled for November 20 at Market Square, with more than 45 local vendors and music. This is an advance notice, not a report that the fair has taken place.
items.why_it_matters: A modest glimpse of local makers, nonprofits and seasonal gathering in one Canadian downtown.

items.headline: How Venice created the first ghetto
items.summary: Historian Alexander Lee reconstructs the Venetian Senate's 1516 decision to confine Jewish residents to a gated island, exploring the mix of exclusion, commercial dependence and state control behind it.
items.why_it_matters: The essay reveals how a local political compromise became a lasting institutional form and word.

worth_your_time.headline: A medieval tooth reveals a surprisingly early industrial pollution problem
worth_your_time.summary: Chemical analysis of medieval English tooth enamel suggests that children in lead-mining communities were exposed to dangerous pollution centuries before the Industrial Revolution. The evidence concerns specific communities, not all medieval England.
worth_your_time.why_it_matters: Biological archives complicate the idea that severe industrial pollution began only with factories.

daily_wonder.title: Earthrise, seen from lunar orbit
daily_wonder.caption: On December 24, 1968, Apollo 8 astronaut William Anders photographed Earth appearing above the Moon's horizon. The rise is an effect of the spacecraft's motion: from a fixed position on the near side of the tidally locked Moon, Earth does not ordinarily rise and set.
daily_wonder.alt: Blue and white Earth suspended against black space above a broad gray lunar horizon.
daily_wonder.credit: William Anders / NASA, Apollo 8; Wikimedia Commons
daily_wonder.rights: Public domain in the United States — work created by NASA

reflection.passage: Far from being the austere censor of desires, I admit, that they often produce charming illusions.
reflection.author: Joseph Droz
reflection.work: The Art of Being Happy, Letter V: Our Desires
reflection.context: Droz argues that the absence of suffering is not enough for a full human life. He recognizes that desire can mislead but also gives imagination and aspiration their force. The English edition is a translation; the translator was not identified in the source checked.
reflection.question: When does an imagined future enrich the present, and when does it pull attention away from it?
